young.html: Herman Melville went to sea as a young man and sailed on a whaling ship in the Pacific. Years later he wrote Moby-Dick, the story of a whaling voyage and a captain who will not give up.

A young man named Ishmael joins the crew of the ship Pequod with his new best friend, Queequeg, a harpooner from a far-off island. Their captain, Ahab, has a leg made of whalebone: on an earlier voyage, a giant white whale named Moby Dick took his leg. Now Ahab wants revenge, and he will chase the white whale around the world.

young.html: The book is also full of facts about whales: how big they are, how they swim, how sailors hunted them in the 1800s for the oil used in lamps. Melville loved whales, even while he wrote about hunting them.

For parents: the novel describes whaling, which was bloody work, and it ends in disaster for almost everyone aboard. Young readers enjoy the early chapters (Ishmael and Queequeg's friendship), the whale facts, and a good abridged edition.

How big is a whale? A large sperm whale like Moby Dick can be about 50 to 60 feet long. Go outside with a tape measure or count steps (one big step is about 3 feet). Mark out 55 feet. How many of your family lying head to toe would fit?

full.html: Herman Melville (1819–1891) grew up in New York; when his family fell on hard times, he went to sea. In 1841 he sailed on the whaler Acushnet, jumped ship in the Marquesas, and returned home years later to write popular adventure books about the South Seas. Moby-Dick (1851), dedicated to his friend Nathaniel Hawthorne, was his most ambitious work. It sold poorly, and Melville died almost forgotten; in the 1920s critics rediscovered it, and it is now often called the great American novel.

full.text: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world.
full.author: Melville
full.ed: Harper and Brothers, New York (first American edition)

full.html: Ishmael meets Queequeg at an inn in New Bedford, and the two become the closest of friends. They hear Father Mapple preach on Jonah and sign on the Pequod, which sails from Nantucket on Christmas Day. Captain Ahab stays out of sight until the ship is well at sea. Then, on the quarter-deck, he reveals the voyage's real purpose: to hunt down Moby Dick, the white whale that took his leg, and he nails a gold coin to the mast as a reward.

full.name: gb-pequod-voyage
full.cap: The voyage and the gams, the meetings with other ships.

full.html: The ship meets nine other ships at sea. Each gam brings news of Moby Dick and a different way of facing him: some captains have lost limbs or crew to the whale; one, the Rachel, is searching for its captain's lost son. Ahab will not stop for anyone.

full.text: "I will have no man in my boat," said Starbuck, "who is not afraid of a whale."
full.author: Melville
full.ed: Harper and Brothers, New York (first American edition)

full.html: Starbuck, the first mate, is brave but sensible; he begs Ahab to turn back, for the sake of the crew and their families. Ahab refuses. After three days of chase, the whale sinks the Pequod. Only Ishmael survives.

full.text: On the second day, a sail drew near, nearer, and picked me up at last. It was the devious-cruising Rachel, that in her retracing search after her missing children, only found another orphan.
full.author: Melville
full.ed: Harper and Brothers, New York (first American edition)

full.html: Between the adventures come chapters on whale anatomy, the classification of whales ("Cetology"), the whiteness of the whale, ropes, oil and paintings of whales. Melville mixes sermon, stage play, essay and science. Some readers skip these chapters; others think they are the book's heart, a way of showing that the whale, and the world, can never be fully known or caught.

Ahab sees in the white whale everything that has wounded and baffled him, and wants to strike back at it. Ishmael, the survivor, looks at the same world with curiosity, humor and friendship. The novel sets these two ways of living side by side.
Reading Moby-Dick as simply "man against nature." Ahab's real struggle is with his own pride and obsession, which drag his whole crew with him. Starbuck and Ishmael show other choices.

items: The Book of Jonah, retold in Father Mapple's sermon, and Job, whose Leviathan the whale recalls.
Shakespeare: Ahab speaks like a tragic hero, and some chapters are written as scenes from a play, with stage directions; Melville was reading King Lear and Macbeth.
Homer's Odyssey and Dante's Ulysses: voyages to the edge of the known world.
Darwin, in this same era, also looked closely at living things to ask what they mean; Melville's "Cetology" mocks and admires the classifiers.

questions: What would you have done if you were Starbuck?
Ishmael and Queequeg became friends even though they came from very different places. What helps people become friends?
Ahab could not let go of his anger. Why is it hard to let go?
Why do you think Melville put so many whale facts in a story?
Is there something you would follow across the world?
